headlines.title: G20 live updates: Palantir's Karp says wealth inequality a 'real issue' for societies
headlines.summary: Follow Day 2 of the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, with Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, and ministers discussing AI, policy and trade.
headlines.article_text: G20 Innovation Ministerial: AI policy live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Artificial intelligence is taking center stage at the G20 gatherings this week. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic Co-Founder Tom Brown and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman highlight the tech-focused guests on Wednesday for day two of the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios are leading the conference, which gathers representatives of the G20 nations , including China, Brazil, Canada, Germany and others. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Tesla / SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were among the tech titans at Tuesday's session. The latest from G20: Palantir's Karp says wealth inequality is a "real issue for our societies" OpenAI CEO Altman says the use of AI is "non-negotiable" Anthropic co-founder praises Trump stance on AI data centers Leaders respond to growing backlash on AI data center buildout Jensen Huang calls AI the "great equalizer" that will democratize intelligence Lutnick says semiconductor tariffs are coming and the companies know it Bessent says companies have done a 'horrendous job' explaining benefits of AI, data centers 8 Min Ago Karp: 'I don't believe in the doom message' of AI Alex Karp, chief executive officer of Palantir Technologies, during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Cornell Watson | Bloomberg | Getty Images Palantir CEO Alex Karp said he expects that AI will come with some disruptive elements, but "I don't believe in the doom message." Karp referenced "a certain company" in the U.S. putting out a daily AI doom message that scared people. The comment seemed to be a reference to Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei, who has penned a number of blogs and made other comments about the risks of AI. "It scares people because there are elements of truth in it," Karp said, "but the elements of truth have been exaggerated to the point where it causes huge political problems." Karp has said in previous interviews that he considers Amodei a friend, but that he disagrees with many of his stances on national security and other matters. —Chris Eudaily 32 Min Ago Karp says wealth inequality is a 'real issue for our societies' Palantir CEO Alex Karp speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Sept. 2, 2026. Matt Ramey | AFP | Getty Images Palantir CEO Alex Karp said that the AI revolution is not 100% good, adding that there are "huge dangers" to the technology as he singled out his concerns about wealth inequality. "I think a big problem we have in this country is: I don't think people are down for me being 20 times wealthier, "It leaves a bad taste in people's mouth," Karp said. He noted that it is a "real issue for our societies." "I come from an academic family," he said. "I'm not even sure how I ended up with all this money." —CJ Haddad 49 Min Ago Karp warns of companies 'exfiltrating' data to AI model makers Palantir CEO, Alex Karp speaks with US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Sept. 2, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Laura Garrison | CNBC Palantir CEO Alex Karp dove further into AI regulation during his fireside chat with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, criticizing countries for not having technical experts leading AI regulation. "My biggest criticism of regulation outside of America is: Please get technical experts to do it," Karp said. He said that currently, the application of regulation is coming from companies looking to deploy large language models. Those companies, he said, are "exfiltrating" a country's alpha to the model providers. "This is anti-sovereignty, and whoever's telling you this works needs to be fired because they are hurting your country," he said. —CJ Haddad 1 Hour Ago Mexico’s economy minister meets with Lutnick on tariffs Marcelo Ebrard Mexico Economy Minister speaking with CNBC from the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, N.C. on Sept. 2nd, 2026. CNBC AI is not the only topic of conversation at the G20 innovation summit. Mexico's economy minister Marcelo Ebrard told CNBC that he met with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in Chapel Hill. The two discussed trade and tariffs, but Ebrard offered no further details on the conversation. The meeting comes amid ongoing negotiations between the two countries on the USMCA. Ebrard, in a post on X , shared a photo with Lutnick and praised the G20 as a "great initiative." —Megan Cassella and Mary Catherine Wellons 2 Hours Ago Palantir CEO Alex Karp says regulation needs to be done by people who understand the issues (L/R) Palantir CEO Alex Karp and US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick speak during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on September 2, 2026. Matt Ramey | Afp | Getty Images Palantir CEO Alex Karp took questions from gathered media ahead of his chat with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and said that AI regulation "hurts the countries that are trying to protect themselves." "One of the biggest problems is it's got to be done by people who understand the issues. And even if people you understand the issues, it's very hard to see the downstream effects. That doesn't mean there should be no regulation," Karp said. "I'm not an anti-regulation person. I'm an unhappy Democrat. I'd like to be a Democrat again. We like regulation, but it's very hard to do in practice," he added. —CJ Haddad 2 Hours Ago Altman warns things could going 'very wrong" if cyber AI risks aren't addressed Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on September 2, 2026. Matt Ramey | Afp | Getty Images Altman called cybersecurity one of the biggest challenges to navigate in the age of AI and one that leaders shouldn't sidestep. "I think some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently," he said. Altman said that falling short in cyber defense and other areas "could set this technology back a great deal." —Samantha Subin 2 Hours Ago Altman: Not adopting AI in your country is like not adopting electricity 100 years ago Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on September 2, 2026. Matt Ramey | Afp | Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman thinks the public won't be talking as much about AI a decade from now — it'll be expected everywhere. "A kid growing up today will never be smarter than AI, but he or she will also never have understood a world where every product and service that they interact with is not really smart and really capable and really helpful," he said. Alman referenced the adoption of electricity multiple times in his comments and drew a line between that and AI. "I think it would be approximately as bad of an idea to say we're not going to have AI in our country as it was to say we're not going to have electricity in our country, you know, back 100 plus years ago," he said. — CJ Haddad 3 Hours Ago Altman says countries have to use AI: 'I think it is non-negotiable' Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on September 2, 2026. Matt Ramey | Afp | Getty Images Altman told the gathered ministers and representatives that countries shouldn't overlook the improvements to daily life poised to come from AI. "I think it is non-negotiable that you have to use it," he said.
